summary: Oxcarbazepine is a carboxamide anticonvulsant structurally related to carbamazepine that acts primarily through its active 10-monohydroxy metabolite (MHD) to block voltage-sensitive sodium channels. It is indicated as monotherapy or adjunctive therapy for partial-onset seizures in adults and children (monotherapy from age 4, adjunctive from age 2). Adults start at 600 mg/day in two divided doses, with adjunctive maintenance around 1200 mg/day and monotherapy up to 2400 mg/day; pediatric dosing is weight-based. Clinically significant hyponatremia (sodium <125 mmol/L) occurs in about 2.5% of patients, so serum sodium should be monitored. Patients of Han Chinese, Thai, Filipino and certain other Asian ancestry should be screened for the HLA-B*1502 allele before starting because it raises the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis. About 25-30% of patients with carbamazepine hypersensitivity cross-react. It is a moderate enzyme inducer and reduces the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives.

moa: The anticonvulsant activity is exerted mainly through the active 10-monohydroxy metabolite (MHD). Oxcarbazepine and MHD block voltage-sensitive sodium channels, stabilising hyperexcited neuronal membranes, inhibiting repetitive neuronal firing and reducing propagation of synaptic impulses. Increased potassium conductance and modulation of high-voltage-activated calcium channels may also contribute.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to oxcarbazepine, any component, or to eslicarbazepine acetate
relative: HLA-B*1502-positive patients (SJS/TEN risk) unless benefit clearly outweighs risk
Hyponatremia or concomitant sodium-lowering drugs (e.g. diuretics, SIADH-inducing agents)
Primary generalized seizures (risk of aggravation, especially in children)
monitor: Skin for rash / serious dermatologic reactions

preg: Plasma levels of the active metabolite MHD may gradually decrease during pregnancy, so patients should be monitored carefully during pregnancy and through the postpartum period, with dose adjustment as needed. Antiepileptic drugs carry a risk of fetal harm; use only when benefit justifies risk and encourage pregnancy registry enrollment.
lact: Oxcarbazepine and MHD are excreted in human milk. Decide whether to discontinue nursing or the drug, weighing the benefit of treatment against the potential risk to the infant; monitor the infant for sedation and poor weight gain.
renal: In patients with creatinine clearance <30 mL/min, initiate at one-half the usual starting dose (300 mg/day given twice daily) and increase slowly to the desired clinical response, because MHD clearance is reduced.
hepatic: No dosage adjustment is needed in mild to moderate hepatic impairment; oxcarbazepine has not been studied in severe hepatic impairment, so use caution.

major: Phenytoin - oxcarbazepine (>1200 mg/day) raises phenytoin levels; monitor and reduce phenytoin dose
Hormonal contraceptives (ethinylestradiol/levonorgestrel) - reduced efficacy; use additional non-hormonal contraception
moderate: Strong CYP3A4 or UGT inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) - lower MHD levels by 25-49%; may require oxcarbazepine dose increase
Sodium-lowering drugs (diuretics, SIADH-inducing agents) - additive hyponatremia
minor: Other drugs associated with SJS/TEN - avoid in HLA-B*1502-positive patients when alternatives exist
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; food does not affect absorption
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; additive CNS depression and sedation
interactions.diagnostics: Associated with decreased serum sodium (<125 mmol/L) and decreases in T4 without change in T3 or TSH; monitor sodium and thyroid function

rare: Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis (higher with HLA-B*1502)
Hematologic events (pancytopenia, agranulocytosis, leukopenia, aplastic anemia)
Decreased bone mineral density / fractures with long-term use
emergency: Severe hyponatremia with seizures, obtundation or coma
SJS/TEN or other severe skin reaction
Anaphylaxis or angioedema with airway compromise

monitoring: Serum sodium (baseline and during maintenance, especially first 3 months or with sodium-lowering drugs)
Skin examination for rash; consider HLA-B*1502 testing in at-risk ancestry before starting
Seizure frequency and signs of seizure aggravation
counsel: Take exactly as prescribed and do not stop suddenly - this can worsen seizures
Report nausea, headache, lethargy, confusion or increased seizures - these may signal low sodium
Seek urgent care for rash, blistering, mouth sores, facial swelling or trouble breathing
Tell your doctor about any past reaction to carbamazepine
Use an additional non-hormonal contraceptive - this drug can make the pill fail
Do not drive or operate machinery until you know how it affects you; avoid alcohol
Report any thoughts of self-harm or mood changes immediately
pk: Store at 25 C (room temperature); suspension - use within recommended period after opening
pearls: Activity is driven by the MHD metabolite, not the parent drug
Hyponatremia (sodium <125 mmol/L) in ~2.5% of patients - most common clinically relevant metabolic effect; check sodium
Screen for HLA-B*1502 before starting in patients of Han Chinese, Thai, Filipino and related Asian ancestry due to SJS/TEN risk
A weaker enzyme inducer than carbamazepine but still reduces hormonal contraceptive efficacy
Can aggravate primary generalized seizures, particularly in children
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered unless it is almost time for the next dose; do not double up. Shake the suspension well before each dose.
overdose: Reported overdoses (up to ~48,000 mg) caused nausea, vomiting, somnolence, agitation, hypotension, tremor, and at higher exposure coma, convulsions, depressed consciousness, diplopia, QT prolongation and decreased urine output; all reported patients recovered. There is no specific antidote; treatment is symptomatic and supportive, with consideration of gastric lavage and/or activated charcoal.
